rewrites.summary:
At roughly 5 a.m. on 26 April 2025 three young men were beaten in a fast-food restaurant in this region's largest city solely because they were gay; the victims were hospitalised, video of the attack later circulated publicly, and the prosecutor's office reconstructed the sequence - insults and threats first, then the physical assault.

A June 2026 press survey of reporting from the region documents a sustained pattern rather than isolated events: rising homophobic bullying, violence against LGBTIA+ people and associated suicides, with multiple cases listed. The pattern is qualitative but official: a hospitalisation-level public assault and a prosecutorial reconstruction sit alongside a growing documented toll.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The June 2026 survey's catalogue covers the region's towns generally — the pattern is continuing across the region rather than isolated to the largest city — and no parent-nation policy turbulence, litigation flux or formal neighbour comparison is recorded for this region in this record.
rewrites.localsOnly: No resident-facing facts distinct from the safety picture — local cultural roles, registration practice or resident data — are recorded for this region in this record.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The June 2026 survey is a press compilation rather than official statistics, so the toll is qualitative; no charging or conviction outcomes beyond the April 2025 incident are recorded, and no trans-specific safety data for this region appear in the record.

rewrites.summary:
In December 2024 this province enacted a package of three laws affecting transgender people as a class: school rules requiring parental notification and consent before staff use a student's gender-related chosen name or pronouns; a prohibition on puberty blockers and hormone therapy for minors; and related vital-statistics amendments. Trans and intersex advocacy organisations said at the time they would continue legal action.

In December 2025 the government invoked the constitutional override clause to shield all three laws from judicial remedy. Two national 2SLGBTQ+ organisations, together with five gender-diverse young people, say the constitutional challenge continues despite the shield - a provincial posture of legislating trans-targeting rules and then placing them beyond the courts.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Litigation flux: two national 2SLGBTQ+ organisations and five gender-diverse young people say the constitutional challenge continues under the override shield.
rewrites.localsOnly: The school pronoun/opt-in rules, the minors' care ban and the vital-statistics amendment bind residents' institutions — a visitor uses their home passport and never touches them; their traveller-facing weight is the climate signal and the street pattern, not the letter of the laws.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Alberta's second-highest provincial 2021 gender-related homicide rate of women and girls (0.68 per 100,000) is a general gendered-violence base-rate proxy, not a trans-specific measure; it should not move a trans-traveller rating.

The outcome of the continuing constitutional challenge is unresolved in this record.

rewrites.summary:
In August 2023 the provincial government announced school policies requiring parents to be asked for permission before staff use a student's preferred name or pronouns (for pupils under 16), parents to be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs to be paused. The province's senior trial court struck the rule down as unconstitutional; the government responded by legislating the consent rule into the Education Act and invoking the notwithstanding clause to immunise it from judicial review.

The matter went to the province's Court of Appeal, which largely allowed the government's appeal in August 2025; a current-status verification found no later ruling, leaving the re-legislated, shielded policy standing. For a visitor the education rule is primarily resident-facing; the durable signal is institutional: a provincial government re-legislating a policy a court had voided and shielding that from rights review - official hostility hardened past ordinary litigation.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Litigation flux: in November 2025 the national Supreme Court agreed to hear the appeals in the school pronoun law challenge — both the province and the LGBTQ+ rights group appealed and asked for an expedited hearing alongside another province's religious-symbols law challenge; no merits ruling has changed the policy, but the constitutionality of the re-legislated, shielded consent rule is now before the country's highest court.

The appeal record also includes an intervenor submission arguing the override clause must align with the nation's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy.
rewrites.localsOnly: The under-16 parental-consent name/pronoun rule, its legislated form (Education Act s.197.4) and the court proceedings around it are school-policy matters facing resident students; visitors encounter them only as a signal of provincial posture toward trans people.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
The 2021 gender-related homicide rate (1.03 per 100k, the highest provincial figure cited) is a non-trans-specific proxy covering women and girls generally and should not be read as traveler-facing trans risk.

The record's sources diverge on the jurisdiction point: one records the appeal ruling as holding that courts lack jurisdiction to test the shielded rule, while another records that a judge may still determine whether the law limits rights; both agree the policy stands.

rewrites.summary:
This region's prosecution system names anti-trans crime as its own charging category: the region's 2021 hate-crime statute created a dedicated transgender-identity aggravation, and the prosecuting authority reported 104 charges carrying it in 2025-26 (up 21% on 86 the year before), while police recorded 8,538 hate crimes in the provision's first full year. For a visitor who is assaulted or harassed, the machinery exists to see the offence counted and charged by name.

The region's parliament passed a more expansive self-declaration gender-recognition law with a two-thirds majority in December 2022 - evidence of markedly more trans-accepting regional institutions; the same nation-wide rules on legal sex and single-sex services apply here as across the parent nation.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Parent-nation turbulence: the central government blocked the self-declaration law with the first-ever use of a statutory veto order; verification as of September 2026 confirms the bill fell and remains not law, with no revival.

Litigation flux: a June 2026 ruling by the region's senior court quashing trans custody guidance stands with no appeal, following a national court ruling (April 2025) on the same question.
rewrites.localsOnly: The blocked Gender Recognition Reform Bill concerns self-declaration birth-certificate procedures for residents; the voided prison guidance determines placement of those in Scottish custody, which residents and any detained visitor share.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The hate-crime figures are recorded-charge and recorded-crime counts; conviction outcomes are not recorded in this record, so enforcement beyond charging is unverified.

rewrites.summary:
The capital recorded the highest transfeminicide toll in the country in 2024 — 17 LGBT+ homicides, of which 11 were trans women — and remains among the highest-count states in 2025. The raw violence data is a negative signal for a visitor, though part of the elevated count reflects the capital's superior reporting infrastructure rather than proportionally higher danger.

Counterbalanced by the strongest institutional response of any Mexican state: transfeminicide was made a distinct crime in July 2024 (“Ley Paola Buenrostro”, the second state to do so); a dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit created in December 2024 covers all violent deaths of trans women; a prosecutor's protocol (Acuerdo FGJCDMX/04/2025) requires feminist-context investigation with immediate-action deadlines; and a new Gender Police launched in August 2025 with 30 patrol units. For a visitor assaulted in the capital there is trained machinery to investigate, where other jurisdictions have none. Modestly above the national score (0.55): the protective and investigative framework is the strongest in Mexico and materially changes what a visitor who encounters violence or discrimination faces after the fact, even though the pre-violence risk data is the country's worst.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Neighbour comparison from the record: the two other high-count jurisdictions cited — Nuevo León and Michoacán (0.40 each) — have no equivalent investigative machinery; this contrast frames how exceptional the capital's response is.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The capital's administrative LGR regime — in force since 2014 and opened to 12-year-olds by a 2021 decree — is a resident-facing civil-registry procedure; visitors never enter it.

The capital retains the country's most protective registration record: gender-identity change permitted since 2008, a conversion-therapy ban since 2020, and non-binary registration added in 2025, all confirmed current as of a September 2026 check.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Two of the record's five sources were not retrievable at fetch time (one returned only site navigation, one a 404), so the transfeminicide-offence reform and the gender-police launch rest on the source summaries rather than on live pages.

rewrites.summary:
The record's core practical-safety signal is the worst in the national data: this state led the national LGBT+ fatality count for four consecutive years — in 2021 alone, 10 recorded violent deaths of LGBT+ people, with 19 of 32 jurisdictions recording victims — and closed 2025 with at least 15 recorded hate crimes; the killing of a 27-year-old trans woman, stabbed to death in a motel on 19 November 2025, came after the state observatory had already counted nine hate crimes earlier that year, three of them against trans women, and the Coatzacoalcos-Oluta corridor is named in the national notes as this state's concentration zone. The danger inside the state is metro-and-corridor concentrated rather than uniform.

Legal protections and enforcement are absent in practice: before the 2025 civil-code gender-identity reform — among the last to be legislated — a visitor or resident had no legal route to correct gender documents, and there is no functioning investigation or prosecution machinery, distinct from other jurisdictions where laws exist but enforcement is weak. Activists cite deliberate filing-away of cases, the state prosecutor's office has lost investigative files entirely, and in one emblematic case (a chef killed in February 2021) the homicide file had simply disappeared; the impunity here is total.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Neighbour comparisons: in 2021 the state's 10 recorded cases placed it ahead of other jurisdictions (Guanajuato 9, Estado de México 7, Chihuahua 6); Guanajuato, a neighbouring jurisdiction that also carries sustained violence, has a comprehensive diversity law and a court-forced recognition procedure, and Nayarit was the first national jurisdiction to type the transfeminicide offence (March 2024).

Reform timing and national context: the state's gender-identity civil-code reform arrived among the last — 22 of 32 jurisdictions had a recognition procedure by March 2025 — and a May 2026 national impunity report ranked this state and Guanajuato joint-second (six killings each) for 2025 LGBT+ deaths nationally, behind a jurisdiction ranked first (seven).
rewrites.localsOnly: The 2025 civil-code gender-identity procedure is a resident-facing civil-registry route for document correction; a trans visitor travelling on home documents never enters it. Resident case data show the backlog: a January 2025 running total put 460 hate-crime cases unresolved, and emblematic cases have arrests but no final sentences.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
General insecurity in the north of the state (municipalities with most internally displaced people from armed-group violence) affects all travellers; it matters here only insofar as it further disables the reporting and investigation channel for anti-LGBT violence.

The 2025 year-end hate-crime figure was readable only as a headline at fetch time, so that count rests on the headline rather than the article body.
